case_name: FSSAI enforcement action against Shivam Agro and TCF Chocolates & Gifts Pvt. Ltd.
citation: FSSAI licence suspension orders, effective 1 October 2026
court: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
holding_summary: FSSAI suspended the food business licences of Shivam Agro and TCF Chocolates & Gifts Pvt. Ltd. with immediate effect after inspections found serious hygiene and safety violations. The TCF Chocolates inspection, triggered by a consumer complaint about a food order placed through an e-commerce platform, found pest infestation, uncovered drainage and expired food colours/flavours stored alongside cleaning chemicals, with an earlier compliance score of only 14%. The Shivam Agro inspection found stagnant sewage water, rodent and pest activity, a non-functional laboratory and labelling irregularities. Both firms were directed to halt all food business operations while the suspension remains in force.
why_it_matters: A reminder that FSSAI can and does act on a single consumer complaint traced through an e-commerce order, and that a prior low compliance score compounds the risk of an immediate licence suspension rather than a lesser penalty.

case_name: Pankaj Chhabildas Sheth v. Abhyudaya Co-Operative Bank Ltd.
citation: (2026) ibclaw.in 1031 NCLAT; also cited as 2026 TAXSCAN (NCLAT) 226
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (Principal Bench, New Delhi)
holding_summary: Pankaj Chhabildas Sheth, a director and personal guarantor of M/s Veer Wires Private Limited, had guaranteed credit facilities extended by Abhyudaya Co-Operative Bank Ltd.; an arbitral award dated 23 June 2023 held the corporate debtor and its guarantors jointly and severally liable for Rs. 4.20 crore plus 14.5% interest. Sheth's Section 94 IBC application seeking his own insolvency resolution was ultimately dismissed by NCLT as an attempt to obtain an interim moratorium and obstruct the bank's lawful recovery and SARFAESI enforcement rather than a genuine bid at resolution and repayment planning. NCLAT dismissed Sheth's appeal, holding Section 94 applications must be pursued in good faith for actual insolvency resolution, not as a shield against creditor enforcement.
why_it_matters: Signals that NCLAT will scrutinise a personal guarantor's Section 94 application for bona fides and will not permit the interim moratorium it triggers to be used tactically to stall SARFAESI or other recovery proceedings — relevant to both guarantors and secured creditors litigating parallel recovery and personal-insolvency matters.

case_name: Serum Institute of India Pvt. Ltd. v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission & Anr.
citation: APTEL, order dated on or about 28-29 September 2026, setting aside MERC order dated 30 May 2019
holding_summary: Serum Institute of India Pvt. Ltd. (SIIPL) operates wind power plants totalling 57.2 MW across Dhule, Sangli and Satara districts in Maharashtra, consuming the power captively and supplying surplus to third-party consumers through Open Access. During April 2016-March 2018, Open Access restrictions prevented delivery of generated power to SIIPL's intended consumers, causing over 3.67 crore units of surplus wind energy to be injected into the state grid instead; MERC rejected SIIPL's claim for compensation by an order dated 30 May 2019. APTEL set aside MERC's rejection and directed MERC to determine, together with applicable carrying costs, the amount payable to SIIPL by Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. for the surplus energy injected during the restricted period.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a captive generator is entitled to compensation for surplus energy injected into the grid when regulatory Open Access restrictions prevent its delivery to the generator's own consumers, reinforcing that a distribution licensee cannot retain the benefit of such injected power without payment.

case_name: State of Odisha and Others v. Dhanurdhar Champatiray
citation: Orissa High Court, decided 21 September 2026 (Routray, J.)
holding_summary: Nine writ petitions challenged orders of District Judges, sitting as appellate authorities under Section 37(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The respondents raised a common preliminary objection that, since the Arbitration Act bars a second appeal against such orders (an appeal lying only to the Supreme Court), the writ petitions were an impermissible substitute for a second appeal. Justice B.P. Routray rejected the objection, holding that the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 is not an appellate remedy and cannot be curtailed by a statutory bar on second appeals, though he confirmed that such supervisory jurisdiction over a Section 37 order remains confined to cases of egregious illegality, perversity or a patent lack of jurisdiction.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a party left without a further statutory appeal after a Section 37 order is not without recourse and can still invoke the High Court's limited supervisory writ jurisdiction, though only in cases of serious jurisdictional or legal error rather than as a routine further round of merits review.

case_name: Sandeep Kumar Bhagat v. Punjab National Bank & Ors.
citation: NCLT Guwahati Bench, decided 10 September 2026
court: National Company Law Tribunal, Guwahati Bench
holding_summary: Three group companies — Shree Sai Prakash Alloys Pvt. Ltd., Shree Sai Rolling Mills (India) Ltd. and Shree Sai Smelters (India) Ltd. — had been funded by Punjab National Bank, were classified as NPAs, went through CIRP, and were ordered into liquidation on 25 January 2024. Sandeep Kumar Bhagat, through his legal heirs, proposed a Rs. 22.50 crore one-time settlement to PNB and alleged the bank failed to consider the proposal despite being notified. The NCLT Guwahati Bench refused to direct PNB to accept the OTS proposal, holding that accepting a one-time settlement is a matter of commercial discretion for the lender and that the Tribunal has no power to compel a financial creditor to accept a settlement that was never crystallised into a binding agreement, particularly once liquidation has already commenced.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a borrower, or heirs acting for one, cannot use the NCLT to force a bank's hand on a proposed one-time settlement once liquidation has begun — accepting or rejecting an OTS remains a commercial call for the lender, not a direction the tribunal will issue.

case_name: In re: Composite Scheme of Arrangement among Parle Products Pvt. Ltd., Parle Biscuits Pvt. Ltd. and Parle Brands Pvt. Ltd.
citation: NCLT, Mumbai Bench, second-motion order dated 23 September 2026 (first-motion order dated 19 June 2026)
court: National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench
holding_summary: NCLT Mumbai's second-motion order sanctioned a composite scheme of arrangement among Parle Products Pvt. Ltd., Parle Biscuits Pvt. Ltd. and newly-incorporated Parle Brands Pvt. Ltd., under which Parle Products' processed-food and captive wind-power undertakings are demerged into Parle Brands, Parle Products is then amalgamated into Parle Biscuits (with Parle Products shareholders receiving 15 equity shares of Parle Brands, plus equity shares and OCRPS of Parle Biscuits, for every 100 shares held), and Parle Biscuits' own processed-food and ancillary business is further demerged into Parle Brands. The bench (Technical Member Prabhat Kumar and Judicial Member Sushil Mahadeorao Kochey) found the scheme fair, reasonable and not contrary to law or public policy, ordered Parle Products dissolved without winding up, and directed the companies to file certified copies of the order and scheme with the Registrar of Companies within 30 days.
why_it_matters: Illustrates the multi-step demerger-cum-amalgamation structure large private groups are using to separate processed-food and ancillary operations from real-estate and brand-holding businesses, including the mixed equity-and-OCRPS consideration mechanics an NCLT will accept as fair in a closely-held group restructuring.

case_name: Breach Candy Swimming Bath Trust & Ors. v. Rajesh Somnath Nerkar
citation: Writ Petition No. 9972 of 2026, decided 1 September 2026
holding_summary: Justice Sandeep V. Marne dismissed a writ petition filed under Article 227 by the Breach Candy Swimming Bath Trust against a Controlling Authority order directing it to pay Rs. 11,67,785 in gratuity (with 10% interest) to its former manager of 23 years, Rajesh Somnath Nerkar, whose services were terminated in 2023 over an alleged Rs. 5 crore loss from shredded membership records. The Court held that the Trust could not bypass the statutory appeal remedy under Section 7(7) of the Payment of Gratuity Act by directly invoking Article 227 after the limitation period for that appeal had lapsed, and that the Trust's absence from the gratuity proceedings (which went ex parte) was of its own making. It imposed Rs. 1 lakh in costs on the Trust.
why_it_matters: A reminder that an employer disputing a gratuity order must pursue the statutory appeal within time rather than seeking a writ as an afterthought, and that unproven loss allegations will not excuse non-payment.

case_name: Amazon Seller Services Private Limited v. Goodluck Buildtech Pvt. Ltd.
citation: O.M.P.(I) (COMM.) 443/2026, Delhi High Court, order dated 28 September 2026
holding_summary: Amazon sought Section 9 interim relief to access and remove its assets from a leased logistics facility (Horizon Urban Logistics Park, Alipur) after terminating its lease with Goodluck Buildtech, which contested the termination citing force majeure. Justice Om Prakash Shukla appointed former Supreme Court judge Justice S. Ravindra Bhat as sole arbitrator for the dispute, which involves an indemnity claim of roughly Rs. 182.50 crore and fixtures/fit-outs worth about Rs. 120 crore, and appointed a Local Commissioner to inspect and inventory Amazon's assets at the premises pending arbitration.
why_it_matters: A practical illustration of how courts use a Local Commissioner under Section 9 to preserve and inventory disputed assets at a leased commercial property while a high-value arbitration is set up, rather than leaving a party to self-help remedies.

case_name: Incyte Holdings Corporation & Anr. v. Melody Healthcare Pvt. Ltd.
citation: CS(COMM) 1054/2026, Delhi High Court, order dated 24 September 2026
holding_summary: Justice Vikas Mahajan granted Incyte an ex parte ad interim injunction restraining Melody Healthcare from making, selling or exporting products containing ruxolitinib, finding a prima facie case of infringement of Indian Patent No. 269841 (valid until 12 December 2026). The Court relied on Melody's listing of 'Ruxolitinib Phosphate' in its API product list and as a supplier on Pharmacompass, and a September 2026 investigation report showing Melody held a Maharashtra FDA manufacturing licence for the API and had developed a generic in-house, treating this as an offer for sale under Section 48 of the Patents Act even absent an actual launch.
why_it_matters: The second ex parte injunction this year over the same ruxolitinib patent (after a similar order against Aurore Life Sciences in July 2026) confirms Delhi High Court's willingness to treat API listings and manufacturing-licence preparations, not just an actual product launch, as sufficient 'offer for sale' infringement to justify an interim injunction ahead of a patent's expiry.

case_name: Sami-Sabinsa Group Ltd. & Ors. and Kerry Inc. v. Union of India, FSSAI & Ministry of AYUSH
citation: Karnataka High Court, interim order (vacation bench)
holding_summary: Health-supplement manufacturers, including Kerry Inc. and a group led by Sami-Sabinsa, challenged an FSSAI advisory (16 April 2026) and a Ministry of AYUSH directive (15 April 2026) restricting use of ashwagandha leaves in supplements, arguing that a restriction of this kind required a formal amendment to the Food Safety and Standards Regulations, 2016 rather than an advisory, and that the underlying studies did not establish a safety risk. Justice S.R. Krishna Kumar, sitting as vacation bench, granted an interim stay of both the advisory and the directive, preserving the status quo for manufacturers and exporters pending further hearing.
why_it_matters: A reminder that FSSAI cannot use an informal advisory to restrict an ingredient already permitted under the 2016 Regulations — any such restriction needs a formal regulatory amendment, giving affected manufacturers a ready administrative-law challenge to similar advisories.

case_name: Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Ltd. (TANGEDCO/TNPDCL) v. Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission & Techno Electric & Engineering Co. Ltd.
citation: Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, order dated 10 August 2026
holding_summary: In a dispute over the Average Power Purchase Cost cap applicable to Techno Electric's 111.90 MW wind capacity in Tamil Nadu, APTEL (Officiating Chairperson Seema Gupta and Judicial Member Virender Bhat) condoned TNPDCL's 632-day delay in filing its appeal against a TNERC order that had ruled for the generator, while directing TNPDCL to pay Rs. 1 lakh in costs to Techno Electric. TNERC had held on 9 July 2024, and clarified on 28 January 2025, that the tariff cap under TNPDCL's April 2022 circular should use the SECI bid tariff of the corresponding year rather than the year of commissioning.
why_it_matters: Shows APTEL remains willing to condone even very long delays by a discom in appealing an adverse tariff order, provided costs are imposed — generators should not assume a long-delayed discom appeal is time-barred as a matter of course.

case_name: Eastern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited v. Daulat
citation: NCLAT, Principal Bench, order dated 25 September 2026
holding_summary: NCLAT (Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma, Judicial Member, with Technical Members Arun Baroka and Indevar Pandey) set aside an NCLT order refusing to recall the 2023 dismissal-for-non-prosecution of a Rs. 20.72 crore electricity-dues claim by a statutory power distribution company, holding that the company's engaged counsel could not simply hand the brief to a junior and stop appearing, and that such deliberate non-appearance by counsel — as distinct from ordinary negligence — should not be visited on the litigant. Invoking Section 238A of the IBC read with Section 5 of the Limitation Act, the Tribunal recalled the dismissal and restored the claim to NCLT for a merits decision.
why_it_matters: Gives claimants in CIRP/liquidation proceedings a basis to seek recall of a dismissal caused by their own counsel's deliberate default, rather than losing a substantial claim purely to a lawyer's conduct.

case_name: Moser Baer Solar Ltd. Liquidator v. JFC Finance (India) Ltd. & Ors.
citation: Supreme Court, order dated 1 October 2026
holding_summary: In the Moser Baer Solar liquidation asset auction, NCLAT had directed the liquidator to immediately refund JFC Finance's Rs. 54 crore deposit after a higher bid (totalling Rs. 168 crore) displaced JFC in a fresh auction, holding the return condition in the auction documents had been triggered. On the liquidator/Committee of Creditors' appeal, a Bench of Justices S.V.N. Bhatti and N.V. Anjaria issued notice and directed the parties to maintain status quo on the deposit pending further hearing, with the dispute centring on whether the liquidator may withhold the deposit until the successful bidder pays the full sale consideration.
why_it_matters: An auction participant's deposit in an IBC liquidation sale is not automatically releasable the moment a higher bid displaces them — the liquidator can press to retain it as security until the new bidder actually completes payment, a point now before the Supreme Court.

case_name: Round Pay Voice Tech v. State of U.P. & Ors.
citation: Allahabad High Court
holding_summary: A show cause notice dated 7 May 2022 under Section 74 of the GST Act had proposed recovery of Rs. 57.60 crore (tax, interest and penalty) for July 2017-March 2018, but the final order dated 5 February 2025 raised the demand to Rs. 59.20 crore, the excess being an additional Rs. 1.60 crore penalty. A Bench of Justices Abdhesh Kumar Chaudhary and Shekhar B. Saraf held the order was ex facie contrary to Section 75(7) of the GST Act, which bars a demand exceeding the amount specified in the show cause notice, rejected the State's argument that statutory interest/penalty could be added regardless of the notice, quashed the order, and remanded the matter for a fresh order after giving the petitioner a hearing on the show cause notice as issued.
why_it_matters: A clean, reusable precedent for any taxpayer facing a final GST order that exceeds the show cause notice amount, however the department tries to justify the excess as 'statutory' interest or penalty — Section 75(7) is applied as an absolute ceiling, not a guideline.

case_name: Darzi (India) LLP & Anr. v. Mr. Akhil Jain
citation: CS(COMM) 1027/2026, Delhi High Court
holding_summary: Justice A.J. Bhambhani granted an ex parte ad interim injunction restraining a clothing business run by the defendant from using the 'Men's Darzi' mark, finding the plaintiff (owner of the 'Darzi' mark) had made out a prima facie case of infringement/passing off and that the balance of convenience favoured an immediate injunction pending further hearing.
why_it_matters: Another example of Delhi High Court's readiness to grant an ex parte injunction against a confusingly similar composite mark at the first hearing itself, without waiting for the defendant's response, where the core element of an established mark is simply prefixed or suffixed with a generic word.

case_name: Sanjay Kumar Singh v. Punjab National Bank & Ors.
citation: Patna High Court, order dated 1 October 2026
holding_summary: A rice mill proprietor who had reached a one-time settlement with PNB's Kutumba branch on 29 December 2021 fixing his liability at Rs. 25.70 lakh, and who claimed to have paid Rs. 20 lakh and offered the balance, sought a writ directing the bank to accept the remaining amount and honour the settlement after the bank refused. Justice G. Anupama Chakravarthy disposed of the writ petition, holding that writ jurisdiction cannot be invoked for recovery-related disputes, including enforcement of a one-time settlement, where an effective alternative remedy exists under the SARFAESI Act, and gave the petitioner liberty to approach the appropriate forum, directing that authority to consider the question of limitation.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a borrower cannot bypass the SARFAESI/DRT route merely by framing a bank's refusal to honour an OTS as a breach to be enforced by writ — the dispute, including whether the OTS is binding, must go through the statutory recovery forum.

case_name: RBI enforcement action against Bank of Baroda
citation: Reserve Bank of India, order dated 30 June 2026, under Section 47A(1)(c) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
holding_summary: The RBI imposed a monetary penalty of Rs. 63.60 lakh on Bank of Baroda for non-compliance with its Fair Practices Code for Lenders and KYC directions, following a statutory inspection of the bank's compliance with regulatory directions.
why_it_matters: Part of a steady drumbeat of RBI enforcement penalties through 2026 on major banks for Fair Practices Code and KYC lapses, underscoring that even large scheduled banks remain exposed to recurring compliance penalties on routine lending-conduct and customer-identification requirements.

case_name: Eastern Division (Projects) Engineers Cooperative Society Ltd. v. State Bank of India & Ors.
citation: Calcutta High Court, order dated on or about 6 October 2026
holding_summary: The ESI Recovery Officer had issued garnishee orders (dated 21 and 26 February 2025) against SBI's Murgasol branch account of the petitioner cooperative society and, when the bank could not remit funds, branded the bank a 'deemed defaulter.' Justice Shampa Dutt (Paul) quashed the garnishee orders, holding SBI could not have remitted ESI dues from what was, on the record, an inoperative account, and that branding the bank a deemed defaulter in these circumstances was without application of mind and violated natural justice. An earlier Division Bench order had allowed the society to operate the account in the ordinary course while keeping Rs. 5 lakh frozen.
why_it_matters: A bank cannot be penalised as a 'defaulter' for failing to comply with a garnishee order against an account that is factually inoperative or frozen — recovery officers must verify the account's actual operability before escalating non-compliance against the bank itself.

case_name: Crystal Crop Protection Limited / FMC India Private Limited (combination notice)
citation: Competition Commission of India, approval reported 1-3 October 2026
holding_summary: The CCI approved Crystal Crop Protection Limited's acquisition of 100% shareholding of FMC India Private Limited, clearing the Indian antitrust leg of FMC Corporation's USD 252 million divestment of its India commercial crop-protection business (agreed 7 May 2026) to Crystal Crop, which also takes a licence to sell FMC-branded crop-protection products in India. The transaction remains subject to other customary closing conditions, with FMC expecting closing by end of 2026.
why_it_matters: One of the larger agrochemical sector consolidations of 2026, relevant to agri-input dealers, distributors and farmers who rely on FMC-branded crop-protection products, since post-closing the Indian distribution/registration holder for those brands changes to Crystal Crop.

case_name: Aayush Bansal & Ors. v. Tata SIA Airlines Ltd.
citation: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Chandigarh, order dated on or about 30 April 2026
court: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Chandigarh
holding_summary: Passengers stranded at Denpasar Airport on their return journey after the airline moved their flight earlier without prior notice, forcing them to buy replacement tickets (about Rs. 51,000) and causing them to miss a connecting Delhi flight, complained of deficiency in service. The Commission enhanced the compensation awarded to Rs. 50,000, affirmed a refund with interest, and awarded litigation costs, holding that timely notice of schedule changes is a basic airline obligation.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that an airline's failure to proactively notify passengers of a preponed (not just delayed) flight is itself an independent deficiency in service attracting enhanced compensation, distinct from ordinary delay-compensation claims.

case_name: Himachal Pradesh Power Transmission Corporation Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission & POWERGRID
citation: Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, order dated on or about 24 July 2026
holding_summary: In a dispute traced to a CERC order of 21 November 2019 approving POWERGRID's Commercial Operation Date for transformer-augmentation assets at the Hamirpur substation, APTEL upheld CERC's order that HPPTCL is liable to bear transmission charges on two 220 kV bays from 31 March 2019 until commissioning of its own associated downstream transmission line, and separately held that the 2016 amendment to the Indian Electricity Grid Code requiring an Implementation Agreement could not be applied retrospectively to the pre-existing arrangement.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a state transmission utility cannot avoid liability for charges on a connected central transmission asset simply because its own downstream works are delayed, and that later IEGC amendments imposing new procedural requirements (like an Implementation Agreement) do not reach back to arrangements predating the amendment.

case_name: S.V. Ramasamy v. [Liquidator], Swastik Spinners
citation: NCLAT, Chennai Bench, order reported on or about 1 October 2026
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), Chennai
holding_summary: Ramasamy, a personal guarantor and promoter of Swastik Spinners, had personally settled the company's dues to its financial creditor Tamil Nadu Mercantile Bank for Rs. 9.50 crore under a one-time settlement, after which the bank accepted payment and issued an account closure certificate; he then sought financial creditor status (and effectively, withdrawal of liquidation) on that basis. NCLAT held he could not claim financial creditor status because there was no assignment of TMB's debt in his favour and he had never sought substitution of TMB in the liquidation proceedings — at most, he could be seen as a promoter who had bought the company's assets in a private sale, not as its financial creditor. An earlier NCLT order (May 2023) rejecting withdrawal of liquidation on the same basis had already attained finality.
why_it_matters: A personal guarantor or promoter who pays off a company's debt out of pocket does not step into the shoes of the original financial creditor merely by virtue of payment — without a formal assignment or court-ordered substitution, the payment buys no standing in the insolvency process.

case_name: [Buyer] v. [Seller] (Greater Kailash property specific performance suits)
citation: CS(OS) 394/2025 and CS(OS) 626/2025, Delhi High Court, order dated 6 July 2026
holding_summary: In connected suits for specific performance of an agreement to sell a Greater Kailash property for Rs. 24.50 crore, where the buyer claimed to have already paid most of the price, Justice Amit Bansal granted an interim injunction and status quo over the property after finding the seller had subsequently sold it to a third party, and directed the seller to deposit Rs. 20.5 crore in court pending final adjudication, expressly noting the observations were only prima facie.
why_it_matters: Shows a practical remedy available to a specific-performance plaintiff facing a seller who has sold the same property to someone else mid-suit: an interim order compelling the seller to secure the disputed consideration in court, rather than leaving the buyer to an eventual, harder-to-enforce damages claim.

case_name: Royal Petro and Chemicals v. State of Rajasthan & Ors.
citation: Rajasthan High Court, 2026
holding_summary: The petitioner challenged a 26 December 2025 Order-in-Original (demand of Rs. 75,38,940 for FY 2021-22, covering excess ITC, non-payment under RCM and return-scrutiny differences), arguing the order was merely uploaded to the GST portal without being effectively communicated, so the limitation period for appeal should not be treated as having run from the upload date. The Court accepted that the appellate authority is bound by Section 107's limitation rules, but held that where the delay arose from circumstances beyond the taxpayer's control — here, lack of effective communication — declining to decide the appeal on merits would cause grave injury and prejudice, and restored the appeal.
why_it_matters: Reinforces a now-consistent line of Rajasthan High Court authority that a GST order merely uploaded to the portal, without some form of effective communication to the taxpayer, does not safely start the appeal-limitation clock — taxpayers who only discover an order late (e.g. via bank account attachment) have a real basis to seek condonation.

case_name: Mahalaxmi Industries v. Union of India
citation: C/SCA/9118/2026, Gujarat High Court, decided 10 July 2026
holding_summary: The petitioner's writ challenged a 23 March 2026 Order-in-Original under Section 74 confirming about Rs. 1.47 crore of ineligible ITC, arguing it had no adequate alternative remedy. The Court rejected the writ, holding the statutory appeal under Section 107 was a fully efficacious alternative remedy, and separately found that the petitioner's counsel had misled the Court by denying that an earlier, withdrawn writ petition by a sister concern (operated by the same persons, in the same industrial park) had challenged the same show cause notice, when the record showed it plainly had.
why_it_matters: A sharp reminder that a writ petition in a GST fraud/fake-ITC matter is likely to be dismissed where a statutory appeal remains available, and that misrepresenting procedural history to the court — such as denying an earlier related petition challenged the same notice — can itself become an independent ground for dismissal.

case_name: Birla Corporation Ltd. v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
citation: Supreme Court of India, decided 23 July 2026
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Augustine George Masih dismissed Birla Corporation's appeal against a Madhya Pradesh High Court decision that had upheld a District Collector's stamp-duty levy on the company's limestone mining lease in Satna, computed on anticipated royalty rather than dead rent. The Court held Madhya Pradesh's 1993 notification prescribing this basis is not ultra vires Section 26 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.
why_it_matters: Confirms that states can validly compute stamp duty on a mining lease by reference to the anticipated royalty yield over the lease term rather than the (typically much lower) dead rent figure, materially affecting the stamp duty payable upfront on executing a mining lease in states with a similar notification.

case_name: National Highways Authority of India v. Kochi Aroor Tollways Pvt. Ltd.
citation: Delhi High Court, decided January 2026
holding_summary: The Delhi High Court dismissed NHAI's challenge to an arbitral award directing it to pay Kochi Aroor Tollways roughly Rs. 12.18 crore for revenue losses sustained on the Edapally-Vyttila-Aroor road stretch in Kerala, attributable to incorrectly fixed toll rates, delay in declaring the Commercial Operation Date, and the cost of issuing free monthly passes to local residents, upholding the tribunal's findings as a plausible reading of the concession terms not open to interference under Section 34.
why_it_matters: Another instance of Delhi High Court declining to re-open a tribunal's factual findings on a toll concessionaire's revenue-loss claim against NHAI — concessionaires with a well-evidenced claim for losses tied to delayed COD or incorrectly fixed tolls have a reasonably settled path to recovery that survives a Section 34 challenge.

case_name: Bangalore Development Authority v. Union of India & Ors.
citation: W.P. No. 14520/2026 (GM-RES), Karnataka High Court, interim order dated 3 June 2026
holding_summary: Karnataka RERA and the state Real Estate Appellate Tribunal had held the Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) was a 'promoter' under Section 2(zk) of the RERA Act over the Nadaprabhu Kempegowda Layout, following complaints from allottees about delays and missing infrastructure. Justice Suraj Govindaraj granted the BDA an interim stay of RERA's applicability to its residential layouts where the preliminary land-acquisition notification predates the RERA Act's commencement, pending further hearing; the broader question of whether RERA applies to statutory development authorities at all remains open and undecided.
why_it_matters: An interim signal, not yet a final ruling, that statutory development authorities developing layouts on land acquired before RERA came into force may be able to resist being treated as a RERA 'promoter' for those specific layouts — allottees in such BDA-type layouts should watch this litigation before assuming RERA remedies are available to them.

case_name: In Re: Karan Adani & B. Ravi (Adani Ports & SEZ) — PMC Projects proceedings
citation: SEBI settlement order, 2026
court: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
holding_summary: Adani Ports & SEZ's CEO Karan Adani and CFO B. Ravi each agreed to pay Rs. 13.65 lakh to settle separate SEBI proceedings concerning the company's PMC Projects dealings, after a panel of SEBI whole-time members approved the settlement terms on 13 August 2026; the applicants confirmed remittance on 5 September 2026 and SEBI confirmed receipt, settling the proceedings without any admission or denial of the underlying findings.
why_it_matters: A further example, alongside the same week's MPS settlements, of how readily key-managerial-personnel-level SEBI proceedings against a major listed group can be closed out through the settlement route once terms are agreed with a whole-time-member panel.

case_name: [Former CEO] v. [Lending Bank] (Reliance Commercial Finance fraud classification)
citation: Delhi High Court, Division Bench (Justices Prathiba M Singh and Madhu Jain), decided March 2026
holding_summary: The Division Bench set aside a bank's 'fraud' classification order against a former CEO of Reliance Commercial Finance, holding the classification could not be sustained because the underlying show cause notice had never actually been served on him. The Court reiterated the settled position that a genuine opportunity to respond to the show cause notice is a mandatory precondition to a fraud classification, while also noting account holders bear a reciprocal duty to keep the bank informed of any change of address.
why_it_matters: Continues a consistent Delhi High Court line (alongside the Akash Gupta and Apple Commodities matters against PNB) holding that a bank's fraud or wilful-default classification cannot stand without proof of actual service of the show cause notice and a real opportunity to reply — a borrower or erstwhile officer facing such a tag should first check whether service can actually be proved.

case_name: State Bank of India v. Umed Singh
citation: 2026 LiveLaw (Del) 639, W.P.(C) 8492/2005, Delhi High Court
holding_summary: Justice Shail Jain upheld the finding that Umed Singh's retrenchment (after roughly 11 months engaged, found to be messenger/peon duties disguised as water-supply bills) violated Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, but held the Labour Court had exceeded its jurisdiction in directing his regularisation into permanent SBI employment, relying on the Supreme Court's Umadevi line of authority and noting Singh had never specifically sought regularisation as relief and that the dispute had lingered over three decades. The Court substituted a lump-sum compensation of Rs. 1 lakh in full and final settlement in place of reinstatement/regularisation.
why_it_matters: A workman who proves an illegal retrenchment under Section 25F is not automatically entitled to regularisation or permanent status merely because the violation is established — tribunals exceed their jurisdiction by ordering regularisation as a remedy where that was never specifically claimed, and courts will substitute compensation instead, particularly after a long-delayed, brief original engagement.

case_name: [Liquidator] v. [Suspended Management] (preferential/fraudulent transaction avoidance application)
citation: 2026 TAXSCAN (NCLT) 202, NCLT Ahmedabad Bench
holding_summary: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed a liquidator's application under Sections 43 and 66 of the IBC seeking to avoid roughly Rs. 2.50 crore in transactions (Rs. 51.79 lakh flagged as preferential and Rs. 1.99 crore as fraudulent in a transaction audit report), holding the application failed because statutory notice of the proceedings had never been properly served on the suspended management of the corporate debtor.
why_it_matters: A transaction audit report flagging preferential or fraudulent transactions is not, by itself, enough to secure an avoidance order — a liquidator must still ensure the suspended board/management is properly served with notice of the avoidance application, or risk the entire application being dismissed on that procedural ground alone, however strong the underlying audit findings.

case_name: [Complainant] v. Medicover Hospitals, Nellore & Dr. Paluru Manohar Reddy
citation: C.C. No. 169/2025, District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kakinada
court: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kakinada
holding_summary: The patient, admitted on 28 February 2025 and who died on 2 March 2025, was alleged to have been given dialysis despite serious cardiac complications without adequate justification. The Commission found Medicover Hospitals, Nellore, and the treating cardiologist liable for medical negligence and deficiency in service, holding they failed to justify administering dialysis to a patient with serious cardiac complications and failed to produce the complete case sheet and treatment records, and ordered them to pay Rs. 99 lakh jointly and severally (plus Rs. 10,000 costs) within 45 days, with 9% annual interest thereafter.
why_it_matters: A hospital's inability to produce complete treatment records/case sheets when challenged is treated as compounding, not merely accompanying, a negligence finding — an incomplete case sheet can itself become central evidence against the treating hospital and doctor.

case_name: N.L. Ravi Shankar & N. Chandrakala v. Telangana RERA & Aparna Infra Housing (re: 'Aparna Sunstone')
citation: Telangana Real Estate Appellate Tribunal, decided 8 June 2026
holding_summary: Two individuals claiming ownership of the land underlying the 'Aparna Sunstone' project sought cancellation of its RERA registration alleging fraud. Chairperson Justice A. Santhosh Reddy and Judicial Member P. Pradeep Kumar Reddy dismissed their appeal and upheld the RERA Registry's order returning their complaint as not maintainable, holding they were not 'aggrieved persons' under Section 31(1) of the RERA Act since they were not allottees, and that their competing title claim over the land was a matter for a civil court, not RERA.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a person disputing a developer's title to project land cannot use a RERA registration challenge as a shortcut to litigate ownership — only allottees or otherwise genuinely 'aggrieved' persons have standing before RERA, and a title dispute must go through the ordinary civil court route.

case_name: [Importer] v. Commissioner of Customs (misdeclared imported fabric)
citation: 2026 TAXSCAN (CESTAT) 124, CESTAT New Delhi Principal Bench
holding_summary: The Tribunal upheld a Rs. 19.53 lakh penalty under Section 114A of the Customs Act, 1962 against an importer found to have misdeclared imported fabric, holding the mandatory penalty provision was correctly applied on the facts.
why_it_matters: A reminder that Section 114A's penalty is treated as mandatory, not discretionary, once misdeclaration is established — importers cannot expect the penalty to be waived or reduced merely by contesting the underlying classification dispute.

case_name: Baxter (India) Private Limited v. Commissioner of Customs
citation: 2026 TAXSCAN (CESTAT) 345, CESTAT Mumbai Bench
holding_summary: The Tribunal allowed full CENVAT credit on specified Rule 6(5) input services even where those services were used in relation to the manufacture of exempt goods, setting aside the demand, interest and penalty the department had raised on the basis that credit should have been proportionately restricted.
why_it_matters: Confirms that the Rule 6(5) list of input services carries full, unrestricted CENVAT credit regardless of whether the output is dutiable or exempt — manufacturers should check whether a disputed input service falls within that specified list before accepting a proportionate-reversal demand.

case_name: [Importer] v. Commissioner of Customs (BIS certification, spare power supply units)
citation: CESTAT, Allahabad Bench
holding_summary: The Tribunal set aside confiscation and penalty imposed on imported spare power supply units, holding the department had wrongly applied the BIS certification requirement to spare components not intended for independent commercial sale, rather than to the finished product the BIS mark is actually meant to cover.
why_it_matters: A useful precedent for importers of spare parts/components used only for repair or as part of a larger finished product: a BIS certification requirement aimed at a finished, independently saleable product should not be mechanically extended to its spares.

case_name: [Taxpayer] v. [GST Department] (interest-only dispute, departmental appeal)
citation: GSTAT, Ernakulam Bench
court: Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT), Ernakulam Bench
holding_summary: Dismissing a departmental appeal, the Bench held that where a GST dispute relates solely to interest (not tax or penalty), the interest amount itself must be considered for applying the Rs. 20 lakh monetary limit prescribed for departmental appeals before GSTAT, rather than treating interest-only disputes as exempt from the threshold.
why_it_matters: Clarifies a procedural point departments might otherwise dispute: an interest-only matter is measured against the monetary appeal threshold using the interest figure itself, giving taxpayers in smaller interest disputes a concrete basis to resist a departmental appeal below that threshold.

case_name: [Taxpayer] v. [GST Department] (Section 129 detention penalty)
citation: GSTAT, Bengaluru Bench
court: Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT), Bengaluru Bench
holding_summary: The Bench held that failure to issue the mandatory final order in FORM GST MOV-09 under Section 129(3) of the CGST Act vitiates the entire penalty proceedings for detained goods/conveyance, regardless of whether the underlying detention itself was otherwise justified.
why_it_matters: A clean procedural defence for a transporter or consignor facing a Section 129 detention penalty: if the department never actually issued the mandatory FORM GST MOV-09 order, the penalty proceedings themselves are vitiated, independent of the merits of the detention.

case_name: K.K. Praveen v. J.M. Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd.
citation: Supreme Court of India, order dated 9 September 2026
holding_summary: The borrower argued that an earlier ex parte Debts Recovery Tribunal decree barred fresh SARFAESI recovery proceedings against him, also challenging the SARFAESI Act's constitutional validity. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition at the admission stage, holding Section 35 of the SARFAESI Act gives it overriding effect over inconsistent laws, so principles of res judicata and merger based on the earlier DRT decree could not be invoked to bar the Act's operation.
why_it_matters: Confirms that an earlier civil/DRT decree in a lender's favour does not exhaust or bar that lender's separate statutory right to pursue SARFAESI enforcement — borrowers cannot rely on an earlier decree's existence alone to block a fresh SARFAESI action.

case_name: [Customs Authority] v. [Liquidator], Metalite Eco Future Labs
citation: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 745 of 2025, NCLAT
holding_summary: Customs had filed a Form B claim (15 December 2023) and then a Form C claim (30 January 2024) seeking to keep bank guarantees/FDRs worth Rs. 89.16 lakh as security for Rs. 1.81 crore in customs duty over unfulfilled export obligations, arguing the instruments should remain earmarked to keep the guarantee alive. NCLAT upheld the NCLT's direction releasing the FDRs/bonds to the liquidation estate, holding that under Regulation 21A of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, Customs' failure to exercise the non-relinquishment option within 30 days of the liquidation commencement date meant its security was presumed relinquished, regardless of its later claims seeking to preserve it.
why_it_matters: A hard deadline warning for any secured creditor (including a government department holding customs/excise bonds as security) in a corporate debtor's liquidation: missing the 30-day Regulation 21A election window presumptively relinquishes the security, however strong the creditor's later arguments for keeping it alive.

case_name: [Insurer] v. [Complainant] (SCDRC pre-deposit receipt filing)
citation: Madhya Pradesh High Court
holding_summary: The State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission had dismissed an insurer's appeal for failing to timely file its pre-deposit receipt. The Madhya Pradesh High Court set aside that dismissal, holding the SCDRC should have considered the insurer's request for additional time to file the receipt rather than treating the delay as fatal to the appeal.
why_it_matters: Gives an appellant before a State Commission (not just an insurer) a basis to resist outright dismissal where it has sought, but not yet been granted, additional time to complete the mandatory pre-deposit formality — the Commission must actually consider such a request rather than dismissing on the bare fact of delay.

case_name: [Developer] v. [Homebuyer] (RERA refund enforcement, interest)
citation: Madhya Pradesh High Court, July 2026
holding_summary: The Court held that a RERA Adjudicating Officer cannot independently determine and award interest at the enforcement stage once the Regulatory Authority has already decided a homebuyer's entitlement to a refund, setting aside a 10% interest award the Adjudicating Officer had separately fixed while otherwise preserving the underlying refund direction.
why_it_matters: Clarifies the division of functions within a state RERA structure: interest on a refund is for the Regulatory Authority to fix as part of its substantive order, not something an Adjudicating Officer can separately layer on at the enforcement/execution stage.

case_name: In re: Scheme of Arrangement between Larsen & Toubro Limited and L&T Realty Properties Pvt. Ltd.
citation: NCLT, Mumbai Bench, order dated 18 August 2026
holding_summary: NCLT Mumbai admitted the first-motion Scheme of Arrangement petition between Larsen & Toubro Ltd. and L&T Realty Properties Pvt. Ltd.; the order was uploaded on 1 September 2026, with the main hearing fixed for 6 October 2026.
why_it_matters: An early-stage procedural milestone worth tracking for stakeholders of either company — admission of the first-motion petition starts the clock toward the second-motion hearing where the scheme's actual terms are examined and (if approved) sanctioned.

case_name: In re: Composite Scheme of Arrangement, PureSoftware Technologies and Happiest Minds Technologies
citation: NCLT, Bengaluru Bench, order dated 29 May 2026
holding_summary: NCLT Bengaluru sanctioned a Composite Scheme of Arrangement between PureSoftware Technologies and Happiest Minds Technologies, completing the merger process between the two companies.
why_it_matters: A completed corporate restructuring in the IT services sector, relevant to clients, employees and counterparties of either company tracking the merged entity's post-scheme obligations and continuity of existing contracts.

case_name: Hindustan Unilever Ltd. & Procter & Gamble v. Rakesh Goyal & Ors.
citation: Delhi High Court, decree dated 28 February 2026
holding_summary: Justice Tejas Karia decreed a long-standing suit against individuals found to be running a large-scale counterfeiting operation in FMCG products bearing HUL and P&G marks, awarding Rs. 2,50,000 in damages along with actual litigation costs and interest. Because exact sales data for the defendants was unavailable, the Court based the damages on the scale of counterfeit goods documented in the search-and-seizure memos rather than the defendants' own (absent) sales records.
why_it_matters: Shows how courts quantify damages in a counterfeiting suit where the infringer's actual sales records are never produced — the scale of goods actually seized during a court-ordered search becomes the practical proxy for assessing damages, rather than the claim failing for want of the defendant's own sales data.

case_name: Height Insurance Services Ltd. v. Employees' State Insurance Corporation
citation: Calcutta High Court, 2026
holding_summary: The Court dismissed a writ petition challenging ESI authorities' show cause notices and a resulting order determining the petitioner's contribution liability, holding the principal employer remains liable for ESI contributions on workers engaged through a contract arrangement.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that routing workers through a contractor does not, by itself, shift ESI contribution liability away from the principal employer — businesses relying on contract staffing should budget for this liability rather than assume the contractor alone bears it.

case_name: Asif Ahmed Siddique v. UCO Bank (re: Nyka Steel guarantee)
citation: NCLAT, order reported 17 August 2026 (upholding NCLT Mumbai order dated 3 February 2026)
holding_summary: Siddique, a personal guarantor, argued his exposure under Deeds of Guarantee dated 12 December 2017 was capped at Rs. 40 crore. NCLAT upheld NCLT Mumbai's admission of UCO Bank's Section 95 petition against him, holding the Rs. 40 crore cap applied only to the principal liability, while the guarantee separately provided for interest at 12.70% per annum running from the date of demand — so the total amount owed could, and did, exceed the capped principal figure.
why_it_matters: A guarantor cannot assume a stated principal-liability cap in a Deed of Guarantee limits their total exposure — where the deed separately stipulates an interest rate running from demand, accrued interest is added on top of the cap, not absorbed within it, and can push total liability well past the capped figure.

case_name: Central Consumer Protection Authority v. Dial4Trade Technologies Private Limited
citation: Central Consumer Protection Authority, order dated 1 September 2026
holding_summary: The CCPA fined e-commerce marketplace platform Dial4Trade Technologies Rs. 10 lakh for unfair trade practices, holding it facilitated the listing and sale of ammonium nitrate (a restricted/regulated input with explosive and agricultural-fertiliser uses) on its platform in violation of consumer protection norms.
why_it_matters: Another instance (alongside the CCPA's earlier action against Flipkart/Amazon/JioMart over an unregistered herbicide) of marketplaces being held directly liable for facilitating the sale of a regulated agri/chemical input, rather than being shielded by their intermediary status — marketplaces carrying agri-input or chemical listings should audit those categories specifically against sector-specific regulatory restrictions.

case_name: [Taxpayer] v. State of Punjab (GST registration cancellation)
citation: Punjab & Haryana High Court, 2026
holding_summary: The Court quashed a GST registration cancellation order, holding the department ignored the taxpayer's written reply to the underlying show cause notice (dated 12 February 2026) before cancelling the registration, which the Court characterised as non-application of mind. Fresh proceedings were permitted only on condition the reply is genuinely considered this time.
why_it_matters: A further addition to the growing body of High Court rulings quashing GST cancellations for procedural shortcuts — a taxpayer who files a substantive reply to a cancellation show cause notice, only to have it seemingly ignored, has a strong basis to have the cancellation set aside rather than having to accept it and start fresh registration from scratch.

case_name: RBI monetary penalty orders against IndusInd Bank Ltd., Northern Arc Capital Ltd., Muthoot MCred Ltd. and Fusion Finance Ltd.
citation: RBI orders dated 14 August 2026 (IndusInd Bank) and mid-August 2026 (the three NBFCs), imposed under Section 47A(1)(c) read with Section 46(4)(i) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (and the corresponding RBI Act provisions for the NBFCs)
holding_summary: RBI imposed a combined Rs 71.20 lakh in penalties after show-cause notices and personal hearings. IndusInd Bank was fined Rs 59.20 lakh (inspection as on 31 March 2025) for paying interest on certain current account deposits and undertaking synthetic securitisation in breach of RBI's directions on interest on deposits and securitisation of standard assets. Northern Arc Capital was fined Rs 6.20 lakh for misstating complaint data in its FY24-25 financial statements and failing to auto-escalate rejected complaints to its internal ombudsman. Muthoot MCred was fined Rs 3.10 lakh for upgrading NPA loan accounts to standard without full recovery of overdue interest and principal. Fusion Finance was fined Rs 2.70 lakh for not conducting the mandatory six-monthly KYC risk-categorisation review.
why_it_matters: A single inspection cycle shows RBI penalising both a scheduled bank and smaller NBFCs for the same category of lapse — paper compliance (disclosure, KYC review, NPA upgrade documentation) rather than customer-facing wrongdoing — underscoring that internal process gaps alone are enough to draw a Section 47A penalty.

case_name: In Re: Mangalam Global Enterprise Ltd. — eight independent directors and compliance officers
citation: SEBI settlement order dated 30 March 2026
court: Securities and Exchange Board of India
holding_summary: SEBI closed show-cause proceedings (notice dated 10 February 2025) against six independent directors and two compliance officers of Mangalam Global Enterprise Ltd. over alleged misstated financials, fictitious accounting entries, misleading related-party disclosures, and diversion of funds to promoter-group entities, after the eight individuals paid a combined settlement amount of about Rs. 1.04 crore without admitting or denying the findings. The order faulted the independent directors for failing to exercise due diligence under the LODR Regulations and the Companies Act, 2013, and held the compliance officers responsible for regulatory-compliance shortcomings; the company itself disclosed the settlement under Regulation 30 of the LODR, noting it was settled by the individuals, not the company.
why_it_matters: A reminder that SEBI will pursue independent directors and compliance officers personally, not just the company or its promoters, for failing to catch misstated financials and improper related-party transactions — board membership and a compliance-officer title carry individual exposure that a settlement payment (not an admission) can close out.

case_name: Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Ltd. v. Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission & Siwana/Haryana wind generator (unrelated res judicata precedent applied in Haryana solar matter)
citation: APTEL judgment dated 18 September 2026
holding_summary: A bench of Officiating Chairperson Seema Gupta and Judicial Member Virender Bhat set aside a Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission order that would have paid a 5 MW solar project in Bhiwani Rs. 6.44/kWh, restoring the Rs. 5.68/kWh rate. The Tribunal found that the prayers in the generator's 2024 and 2025 tariff petitions were identical, and that HERC's earlier dismissal of the 2024 petition had never been challenged and so was final; the 2025 petition seeking the higher rate on the same facts was therefore barred as res judicata.
why_it_matters: Generators who lose a tariff petition and let the order go unchallenged cannot simply re-file an identical claim later hoping for a different regulatory bench — APTEL will treat an unappealed dismissal as final and bar a second attempt on the same facts.

case_name: Mehta & Modi Realty Kowkur LLP v. Deepa Suraj Premi & Anr.
citation: T.A. No. 45 of 2025, Telangana Real Estate Appellate Tribunal, judgment dated 6 May 2026
holding_summary: The Tribunal upheld a roughly Rs. 11 lakh penalty on the developer of the Greenwood Heights project (Kowkur) for executing sale agreements with homebuyers that were materially different from the standard draft agreement it had uploaded to the Telangana RERA portal at project registration, in breach of Rule 38 of the Telangana RERA Rules. It treated the conduct as furnishing false information and deliberate suppression of material facts, upheld the penalty under Section 60 of the RERA Act, and also upheld directions barring the developer from charging GST on delayed-payment interest and requiring it to dissolve the Greenwood Welfare Association and complete pending works before handing over possession.
why_it_matters: Developers cannot treat the agreement uploaded at RERA registration as a mere formality — executing a materially different sale agreement with actual buyers is independently penalised as false information/suppression under Section 60, on top of whatever relief the buyer separately obtains for the underlying contractual breach.

case_name: [Co-operative Sugar Factory] v. [Workman] (re: dismissal for 240-day unauthorised absence)
citation: Bombay High Court, order dated 7 July 2026
holding_summary: Justice Sandeep Marne, hearing a co-operative sugar factory's challenge to Labour Court and Industrial Court orders, held that dismissing a clerk with 16 years of service over a 240-day unauthorised absence was 'shockingly disproportionate' punishment. Rather than restore the lower courts' reinstatement-with-back-wages relief, the Court substituted a lump-sum payment of Rs. 15 lakh in full and final settlement.
why_it_matters: Even a lengthy unauthorised absence will not automatically justify dismissal where the employee has long service; but courts are increasingly substituting a calibrated lump sum for reinstatement-with-back-wages, so employers facing a disproportionality challenge should weigh a negotiated lump-sum exposure rather than assume full reinstatement is the only risk.

case_name: BRD Finance Ltd. v. Santhosh P.
citation: 2026 LiveLaw (Ker) 459, Kerala High Court, judgment dated 10 August 2026
holding_summary: Justice Easwaran S. allowed a second appeal and set aside the judgments of both the Munsiff Court, Chavakkad, and the first appellate Sub Court, holding that once the State had designated Sub Courts as Commercial Courts (by notification of 24 February 2020) for recovery claims exceeding Rs. 3 lakh under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, a civil court could no longer adjudicate such a specified-value dispute on its merits; the suit (a roughly Rs. 3.47 lakh promissory-note recovery by a kuri company) ought to have been transferred to the designated Sub Court. The Court held the defect carried forward and vitiated the appellate proceedings even though the appellant itself had not raised the jurisdiction objection earlier, and ordered the suit transferred to the Principal Sub Court, Thrissur, with a refund of court fees paid before the higher fora.
why_it_matters: A commercial dispute crossing the specified-value threshold must go to a designated Commercial Court once the State notification is in place — and that jurisdictional defect is not cured merely because neither party raised it at the first opportunity, so it can unwind years of litigation in the wrong forum.

case_name: Shivam Traders and Hire Purchase Pvt. Ltd. v. Madhusudan Vehicles Pvt. Ltd.
citation: 2026:AHC:67074, Allahabad High Court, order dated 31 March 2026
holding_summary: Justice Sandeep Jain held that a civil suit could not be maintained over a dispute concerning premature repayment of a Rs. 19.25 crore long-term loan taken by one NBFC from another in 2019, because Section 45QA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, read with Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013, confers exclusive jurisdiction over such disputes on the NCLT. The civil suit was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
why_it_matters: Disputes between NBFCs (and likely banks) over loan repayment terms governed by RBI directions cannot be litigated in an ordinary civil court merely because the dispute is framed as a contractual one — Section 45QA routes it exclusively to the NCLT, so filing in civil court risks a jurisdictional dismissal years into the litigation.

case_name: [Resolution Professional] v. [Operational Creditor] (re: Crystal Clear Veg Oil Refinery CIRP fee dispute)
citation: NCLAT, order reported March 2026
holding_summary: The NCLAT set aside an NCLT Mumbai order that had unilaterally cut a Resolution Professional's fee in the Crystal Clear Veg Oil Refinery CIRP from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 10,000 per month, and remanded the matter. The Tribunal held that the Adjudicating Authority can fix an IRP's or RP's fee only where the applicant who initiated the CIRP has not itself proposed a fee; where a fee has been proposed, exclusive power to fix the Resolution Professional's remuneration lies with the Committee of Creditors, and the NCLT cannot substitute its own figure for the CoC's.
why_it_matters: An Adjudicating Authority's general supervisory role over a CIRP does not extend to second-guessing a Resolution Professional's fee once the Committee of Creditors has exercised its power to fix it — resolution professionals facing an unfavourable NCLT fee order have a clear basis to appeal where a fee proposal was already before the CoC.

case_name: Yellala Jagadeeshawara Reddy v. ICICI Lombard General Insurance Co. Ltd.
citation: CC No. 156/2025, District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kurnool, order dated 1 October 2026
court: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kurnool
holding_summary: The Commission (President Karanam Kishore Kumar) held ICICI Lombard liable for deficiency in service for repudiating a Rs. 50 lakh life insurance claim on the ground of alleged misrepresentation of facts, after finding no evidence that the insurer's document requests to the claimant had actually been dispatched or served. The insurer was directed to pay the full sum assured.
why_it_matters: Part of a recurring pattern at the Kurnool commission (which has issued similar rulings against ICICI Lombard and HDFC Life on other Rs. 50 lakh claims): an insurer repudiating a claim for non-compliance with document requests must affirmatively prove those requests actually reached the claimant, not merely assert that they were sent.

case_name: Dhanuka Agritech Ltd. v. Union of India & Ors. (re: Crystal Crop Protection's Halosulfuron Methyl registration)
citation: LPA 215/2023, Delhi High Court, judgment dated 29 May 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices C. Hari Shankar and Om Prakash Shukla, on a competitor's (Dhanuka Agritech's) letters patent appeal, quashed the Registration Committee's grant under Section 9(3) of the Insecticides Act, 1968 of a registration certificate to Crystal Crop Protection Ltd. for importing Halosulfuron Methyl 98% and manufacturing Halosulfuron Methyl 75% WG domestically. The Court found the grant manifestly illegal: Crystal Crop's 2011 trial-import permit covered samples from a Singapore supplier, but its 2016 registration application named a different manufacturer (Jiangsu Agrochemicals), which had only been granted temporary registration to manufacture the 98% material in October 2018 — after the relevant approval — leaving no evidence the Registration Committee had any basis to approve the 2016 application as it did.
why_it_matters: A competing manufacturer has standing to have a rival's pesticide/insecticide registration quashed by writ where the Registration Committee approved it without evidence the named overseas manufacturer was actually authorised to produce the active ingredient at the relevant time — registration data mismatches between the trial-import stage and the commercial registration stage are a live, litigable vulnerability, not a mere paperwork formality.

case_name: Dr. Sajan Kurien Mathew v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
citation: Madhya Pradesh High Court, judgment dated 26 May 2026
holding_summary: The Court quashed the termination of an assistant professor that rested on a disciplinary inquiry conducted by an outside officer, holding that allegations of workplace sexual harassment can only be inquired into by the Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) or Local Complaints Committee (LCC) constituted under the POSH statutory framework, and that a disciplinary authority cannot run a parallel inquiry through an outside officer to arrive at the same factual findings.
why_it_matters: An employer facing a sexual harassment allegation cannot route the fact-finding through its ordinary disciplinary machinery instead of (or parallel to) the statutorily mandated ICC/LCC — any termination built on findings from the wrong inquiry body is vulnerable to being quashed regardless of how serious the underlying allegation was.

case_name: FSSAI prohibition/enforcement action against Vatave Health Care (FOLINEURO Syrup) and Global Healthfit Retail India (Neuherbs TRUE VITAMIN)
citation: FSSAI prohibition orders dated 30 July 2026
court: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
holding_summary: FSSAI issued a prohibition order against Vatave Health Care's 'FOLINEURO Syrup – Folinic Acid Syrup', finding the brand name combined with a brain imagery on the pack created a misleading impression that the product supports brain/neurological function, and that it was marketed under a 'Nutritional Food Supplement' category that does not exist under the Food Safety and Standards (Health Supplements and Nutraceuticals) Regulations, 2016. Separately, FSSAI halted sale of Global Healthfit Retail India's 'Neuherbs TRUE VITAMIN' over its trade name, holding the term 'True Vitamin' is undefined and unrecognised under the 2018 Advertising and Claims Regulations and the 2020 Labelling and Display Regulations and could mislead consumers; that company was directed to remove the claims from labels/ads and file an Action Taken Report within 30 days.
why_it_matters: FSSAI is treating a misleading brand name or imagery itself — not just the product's physical safety or composition — as independently actionable where it implies an unauthorised health/therapeutic benefit or uses an undefined marketing term, and will act even where the product's underlying ingredients are not alleged to be unsafe.

case_name: IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. v. Manish Jain & Ors.
citation: CS(COMM) 800/2025, Delhi High Court, order dated 23 March 2026 (2026 SCC OnLine Del 1241)
holding_summary: Justice Mini Pushkarna dismissed the defendant's appeal against a Joint Registrar's order closing his right to file a written statement. The 120-day statutory period for filing a written statement in a commercial suit had expired on 3 December 2025; the defendant's Order VII Rule 11 CPC application (seeking rejection of the plaint) was filed only on 14 December 2025, after that period had already lapsed. The Court held that merely filing an Order VII Rule 11 application after the written statement deadline has passed does not revive or extend that already-lapsed period — a defendant may choose to seek rejection of the plaint before filing a written statement, but cannot use that procedural choice as a device to recover time already lost. A separate argument that an IBC Section 96 interim moratorium barred the suit was left to be decided within the pending Order VII Rule 11 application itself.
why_it_matters: In a Commercial Courts Act suit, the 120-day written-statement deadline is strictly enforced — filing an Order VII Rule 11 application does not pause or restart that clock, so a defendant who has let the deadline lapse cannot use a plaint-rejection application as a backdoor way to buy more time to file.

case_name: Karan Pradeep v. MakeMyTrip (India) Pvt. Ltd. & Malaysia Airlines
citation: South Delhi District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-II, order dated 2 February 2026
court: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-II (South Delhi)
holding_summary: The Commission directed Malaysia Airlines to refund Rs. 65,802 (with 6% annual interest from the original 13 March 2020 travel date) for a cancelled flight, and held MakeMyTrip liable for deficient service and false assurances, imposing Rs. 25,000 against it; both were held jointly and severally liable for Rs. 30,000 in compensation for mental agony. The Commission rejected the argument that an online travel portal is a mere 'facilitator' immune from liability, noting the consumer was made to shuttle between the booking platform and the airline seeking his refund. All amounts carry 8% interest if unpaid within three months.
why_it_matters: Online travel agents cannot hide behind a 'we're just a facilitator' defence when a consumer is bounced between the platform and the airline over a refund — the platform's own conduct in handling (or mishandling) the refund request is independently actionable as a deficiency in service.

case_name: [Four Homebuyers] v. [Developer] (Bengaluru project, missing amenities)
citation: Karnataka Real Estate Regulatory Authority, order dated 4 September 2026
holding_summary: Karnataka RERA awarded four homebuyers, who had each paid roughly Rs. 2.08 crore for their flats, a combined Rs. 10 lakh in compensation after a joint inspection (conducted May 2026) established the developer had not delivered amenities (including a gym and badminton court) that were promised in the project brochure, allotment letters and agreements. The Authority held that a promoter's contractual documentation cannot simply be drafted or relied upon to declare obligations fulfilled when the physical inspection shows otherwise, and rejected a technical defence based on a mismatched project registration number as no bar to an otherwise valid complaint.
why_it_matters: A developer cannot defeat an amenity-shortfall complaint on a paperwork technicality (like a registration-number mismatch), and marketing materials — brochures and allotment letters, not just the final agreement — are treated as binding representations of what a buyer is owed once a physical inspection confirms the shortfall.

case_name: In re: Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited (Section 43A proceedings — Thriveni Earthmovers and Infra combination)
citation: CCI order dated 8 September 2026 (Section 43A, Competition Act, 2002)
holding_summary: The CCI imposed a penalty of Rs. 15 lakh on Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited under Section 43A of the Competition Act, 2002 for breaching the standstill obligation under Section 6(2A) in relation to its combination involving Thriveni Earthmovers and Infra Private Limited, a transaction the CCI had separately approved on 13 May 2025. Lloyds disclosed the order to stock exchanges on 10 September 2026, stating the penalty was not material to its financials and that it intended to comply within the stipulated timeline.
why_it_matters: It is a reminder that the CCI penalises standstill (gun-jumping) breaches as a strict, civil-liability matter under Section 43A regardless of whether the underlying combination was itself later approved, so acquirers must keep completion steps on hold until clearance even in otherwise unobjectionable deals.

case_name: Victorinox India Pvt Ltd v. New India Assurance Co Ltd
citation: Consumer Complaint, South Mumbai District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, decided 2 September 2026
court: South Mumbai District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
holding_summary: The Commission directed New India Assurance to pay Victorinox India Rs. 8,06,49,573 (the net loss figure recorded by the insurer's own surveyor) with 9% interest from the date of the complaint, plus Rs. 50,000 each for mental distress and litigation costs, over a fire that damaged Victorinox's customs-bonded warehouse on 16 February 2019. The insurer had repudiated the claim in January 2021 citing non-submission of certain internal agreements and invoices; the Commission held the rejection was made 'solely on technical ground in a mechanical manner' without substantive justification.
why_it_matters: It reinforces that an insurer cannot repudiate a fire claim over a technical documentation lapse once its own surveyor has quantified and not disputed the loss, and signals continuing exposure for 'mechanical' repudiations under consumer law.

case_name: Haryana Power Purchase Centre v. Siwana Solar Power Projects Ltd (and connected HERC tariff proceedings)
citation: Appellate Tribunal for Electricity order dated 18 September 2026, setting aside HERC order in Petition No. 78 of 2025
holding_summary: A bench of Officiating Chairperson Seema Gupta and Judicial Member Virender Bhat set aside a May 2026 HERC order that had directed HPPC to pay Siwana Solar Power Projects Ltd (a 5 MW Bhiwani solar project) a revised tariff of Rs. 6.44/kWh with 9.15% interest. APTEL held the tariff question was already finally decided: Siwana's 2024 petition seeking the same relief was dismissed by HERC in November 2024 on res judicata grounds and never challenged, so the earlier Rs. 5.68/kWh rate continued to bind the parties and HERC could not revisit it in the later petition.
why_it_matters: It is a reminder to power generators that an unappealed dismissal of a tariff petition forecloses a second attempt at the same relief, even where a sympathetic regulator later appears willing to reconsider the rate.

case_name: Gaurav Jain & Anr. v. Joint Commissioner (Appeals-II), CGST Delhi Zone & Anr.
citation: W.P.(C) 8414/2026; reported as 2026:DHC:6124-DB, Delhi High Court
holding_summary: The petitioners were issued a show cause notice dated 25 June 2025 under Section 122(1A) of the CGST Act proposing only a personal penalty, with the penalty confirmed by an Order-in-Original dated 16 December 2025. A Division Bench held that the right of appeal vests on the date the show cause notice is issued, not on the date of the Order-in-Original or the appeal filing, so the 10% pre-deposit requirement for penalty-only appeals (introduced by the amendment to the proviso to Section 107(6) of the CGST Act with effect from 1 October 2025) could not be applied to a notice issued before that date.
why_it_matters: Gives a taxpayer facing a penalty-only GST order a concrete basis to resist the 10% pre-deposit demand whenever the underlying show cause notice predates 1 October 2025, regardless of when the final order or appeal itself was filed.

case_name: Chattar Singh v. Executive Engineer, HPSEBL & Ors.
citation: CWP No. 8209 of 2026, Himachal Pradesh High Court, decided 16 September 2026
holding_summary: The petitioner's daily-wage engagement with HPSEBL's Rajgarh Division was terminated with effect from 12 March 1997; a Labour Court award dated 27 November 2024 found the termination illegal and ordered reinstatement with seniority and continuity of service, but refused back wages. The High Court set aside the denial of back wages, holding that once a workman pleads he remained unemployed after termination, the burden shifts to the employer to prove he was gainfully employed during the intervening period, which HPSEBL had not done, and directed HPSEBL to pay 50% back wages with up-to-date interest within six weeks.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that an employer cannot avoid back wages merely because a long gap has passed since termination — once the workman pleads non-employment, the employer must affirmatively prove gainful employment elsewhere or pay up.

case_name: RBI enforcement action against Punjab National Bank (currency chest penalties)
citation: Reserve Bank of India penalty orders dated 9 and 11 September 2026 under RBI's Master Directions on Currency Chests; disclosed by PNB on 14 October 2026
holding_summary: RBI imposed four separate monetary penalties on Punjab National Bank totalling about Rs 8.6 lakh for non-compliance with its Master Directions on currency chest operations: Rs 2,91,750 on 9 September 2026, and Rs 1,33,800, Rs 1,34,600 and Rs 2,99,600 on 11 September 2026. PNB disclosed the penalties to the stock exchanges only on 14 October 2026, explaining that the amounts had been directly debited from its account with RBI and were identified during periodic reconciliation, which caused the delay in disclosure.
why_it_matters: Another entry in a recurring pattern of RBI penalties on PNB for currency chest lapses through 2026, and a reminder that such penalties can be debited directly from a bank's RBI account well before the bank discloses them to the market.

case_name: Amba Grains Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. v. Amit Agrawal, RP of Mastana Foods Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
citation: NCLAT, Principal Bench, New Delhi, decision reported 14 October 2026 (connected appeals including CA (AT) (Ins) No. 4257 of 2025 in CP(IB) No. 630 of 2019)
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), Principal Bench, New Delhi
holding_summary: Mastana Foods Pvt. Ltd. had been admitted into CIRP in September 2019 on an SBI petition, and NCLT Delhi later approved a Rs. 135.39 crore resolution plan from a consortium of HR Commercials Pvt. Ltd. and Crown Steels. A rival bidder, Amba Grains Pvt. Ltd., and the corporate debtor's suspended directors filed five connected appeals challenging the plan's approval, raising the conduct of the e-bidding process, a post-bid clarification sought on treatment of Haryana VAT/Excise dues, and the Committee of Creditors' refusal to consider a higher revised offer from Amba Grains. NCLAT dismissed all five appeals, holding that its review of a CoC-approved plan is confined to compliance with Section 30(2) of the IBC and does not extend to re-appraising the CoC's commercial wisdom, and separately held that a plan clause using the word 'may' made formation of a special purpose vehicle optional rather than mandatory for the successful resolution applicant.
why_it_matters: A disappointed bidder cannot use an appeal against plan approval to re-litigate the CoC's commercial choice between competing offers or to challenge discretionary (as opposed to mandatory) implementation steps in the approved plan — NCLAT's review stays confined to the statutory compliance checklist in Section 30(2).

case_name: SEBI (Settlement of Administrative and Civil Proceedings) Regulations, 2026
citation: SEBI Gazette notification, issued on or about 6-7 October 2026, coming into force 7 November 2026
court: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
holding_summary: SEBI notified a new Settlement of Administrative and Civil Proceedings Regulations, 2026, which will repeal and replace the existing 2018 settlement framework with effect from 7 November 2026, subject to transitional and savings provisions for applications already pending under the 2018 regulations. Reported changes include a formula-based settlement-amount calculation, fast-track treatment for smaller matters, and minimum settlement amounts (reported as roughly Rs. 3 lakh for first-time applicants and Rs. 7 lakh for others), alongside stricter debarment consequences for non-compliance with settlement terms.
why_it_matters: Entities currently negotiating or planning a SEBI settlement should factor in the new formula-based amount calculation and stricter debarment terms taking effect from 7 November 2026, and confirm which framework (2018 or 2026) will govern a pending or contemplated application under the transitional provisions.

case_name: In Re: Adani Enterprises Ltd., Adani Green Energy Ltd., Adani Total Gas Ltd., AWL Agri Business Ltd. & Adani Energy Solutions Ltd. (SEBI settlement)
citation: SEBI settlement order, proceedings closed 22 September 2026
court: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
holding_summary: SEBI's adjudication proceedings against five Adani group companies, arising from its examination of related-party-transaction disclosure and audit-certification issues flagged after the Hindenburg Research report, were closed by settlement after the companies paid a combined Rs. 1.5 crore (Adani Enterprises Rs. 76.05 lakh for alleged non-disclosure of certain related-party transactions and audit/limited-review reports signed by a firm without a valid Peer Review Certificate; Adani Green Energy Rs. 45.50 lakh; and Adani Total Gas, AWL Agri Business and Adani Energy Solutions Rs. 9.75 lakh each over reports signed by firms lacking a valid Peer Review Certificate). The companies paid without admitting or denying the findings, and SEBI expressly reserved its right to act further if any submission is later found false or a settlement condition is breached.
