why_it_matters: A reminder that an issuer's related-party-transaction disclosures and the Peer Review Certificate status of the firm signing its audit or limited-review reports are both independently checked by SEBI, and that a lapse on either front can draw a separate adjudication and settlement even where no restatement or fraud finding is involved.

case_name: Percept Talent Management Pvt. Ltd. & Percept D'Mark (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Sourav Ganguly
citation: Calcutta High Court Division Bench judgment dated 16 April 2026 (Justices Debangsu Basak and Md. Shabbar Rashidi), Section 37 appeal dismissed; Supreme Court subsequently dismissed Percept's SLP (bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana)
court: Calcutta High Court (Supreme Court dismissed the SLP against it)
holding_summary: The Supreme Court dismissed Percept's special leave petition challenging the Calcutta High Court's dismissal of its Section 37 appeal, leaving intact a 2018 arbitral award of Rs. 14.49 crore plus 12% annual interest (from 21 November 2007) and Rs. 50 lakh in costs in favour of former cricketer Sourav Ganguly. The High Court had held Percept lost its right to terminate its 2003 player-representation agreement by waiting too long to exercise it and by continuing to act as Ganguly's agent afterward, and separately upheld the tribunal's finding that Ganguly's Kolkata Knight Riders earnings fell outside the parties' revenue-sharing clause.
why_it_matters: A further example of the narrow scope for interference with an arbitral award under Section 37/Article 136, and a reminder that a contractual termination right can be lost by delay and continued conduct inconsistent with having terminated, independent of the merits of the underlying dispute.

case_name: Andavar Transport v. Deputy State Tax Officer
citation: W.P. Nos. 21226 & 21227 of 2026, Madras High Court, order dated 22 June 2026
holding_summary: A goods transporter faced two separate GST assessment orders (dated 26 April 2024 and 13 August 2024) under Section 73 for the same tax period, 2019-20, despite having reversed the disputed input tax credit from its electronic credit ledger under the first order. Justice C. Senthilkumar Ramamoorthy, with the department's counsel not disputing that both orders covered the same issue, quashed the duplicate order and remanded the matter for fresh adjudication, directing the department to grant a hearing and pass a fresh order within three months.
why_it_matters: Continues a consistent Madras High Court line that two GST orders covering the same tax period and the same alleged default cannot both stand — a taxpayer facing a second, overlapping assessment for a period already covered by an earlier order has a straightforward quashing-and-remand remedy.

case_name: Tetra Technologies Inc. v. Union of India
citation: W.P.(C)-IPD 33/2024, Delhi High Court, order dated October 2026
holding_summary: The Patent Office had treated Tetra Technologies' national-phase patent application as abandoned under Section 21(1) of the Patents Act, 1970 after it did not respond to a First Examination Report said to have been e-mailed to its agent in October 2021; the applicant said neither it nor its agent ever received that e-mail and learned of the abandonment only in April 2023 while checking the application's status online. Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav held that a bare record of dispatch of a system-generated e-mail, without proof the e-mail was actually delivered, cannot by itself establish abandonment, since abandonment requires a conscious act or manifest intention on the applicant's part. The Court revived the application, directed the Patent Office to re-send the First Examination Report to the applicant's agent at both postal and e-mail addresses within a week, and granted eight weeks thereafter to respond.
why_it_matters: Gives applicants a concrete precedent to challenge a deemed-abandonment where the Patent Office cannot prove actual delivery of a system-generated FER e-mail, rather than merely dispatch — useful wherever a lapsed response deadline is blamed on a missed e-mail.

case_name: Bhadrashree Steel and Power Limited v. State of Maharashtra
citation: Writ Petition No. 1094 of 2022, Bombay High Court, order uploaded 15 October 2026
holding_summary: Bhadrashree Steel & Power had bought land and a building for about Rs. 8.03 crore (part of a roughly Rs. 13.01 crore total bid) as the successful bidder in an e-auction held by the liquidator of Harneshwar Agro Products Power and Yeast (India) Ltd. under the IBC; the stamp authorities valued the property far higher (first at Rs. 41.96 crore, later revised to Rs. 35.70 crore) under the Annual Statement of Rates and demanded stamp duty on that basis. A Division Bench of Justices Bharati Dangre and Manjusha Deshpande rejected the State's argument that the NCLT is not a 'civil court' for the purposes of Article 16, Schedule I of the Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958, holding that an NCLT acting as adjudicating authority under the IBC falls within that term; finding the e-auction (with 16 interested bidders) transparent and free of any sign of deliberate undervaluation, the Court directed that stamp duty be levied on the actual auction value of Rs. 8.03 crore and that the sale documents be registered accordingly.
why_it_matters: Gives purchasers at NCLT-supervised liquidation auctions in Maharashtra a clear basis to resist stamp duty demands pegged to Ready Reckoner/ASR valuations where the auction itself was transparent and competitive, rather than the (often much higher) government guidance value.

case_name: In Re: Anti-Competitive Conduct by Agro Input Dealers Association and Agro Input Welfare Association
citation: Case No. 06 of 2023, CCI order dated 21 August 2026
holding_summary: CCI found the Agro Input Dealers Association (AIDA), the Agro Input Welfare Association (AIWA), and several named office-bearers liable under Section 3(3)(b) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002 for orchestrating a boycott against the online sale of agri-input products, with AIDA acting as the principal platform through which the boycott was initiated and AIWA substantially implementing it in Gujarat. The individual office-bearers were separately held liable under Section 48 for the associations' contravention. The Commission issued cease-and-desist directions under Section 27(a), imposed monetary penalties ranging from roughly Rs 8,600 to about Rs 5 lakh across the different parties, and under Section 27(g) directed them to organise a competition-law compliance training programme.
why_it_matters: Confirms that trade and dealer associations — and the office-bearers who run them — face direct CCI liability under Sections 3(3)(b) and 48 when they coordinate boycotts of online retail channels, a recurring friction point as e-commerce expands into regulated input markets like agriculture.

case_name: Chhaganbhai Kohyabhai Pateliya & Ors. v. State of Gujarat & Ors.
holding_summary: Gujarat Irrigation Department workers initially engaged as daily wagers, who had converted to permanent status after ten years of service under a 1988 state government resolution, retired on 30 June and were denied the annual increment that fell due the next day. A Single Judge upheld their claim relying on the Court's earlier ruling in KPTCL v. C.P. Mundinamani, but a Division Bench reversed. The Supreme Court (Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva) restored the Single Judge's view, holding that the workers' original daily-wage status could not be used to deny them the notional retirement-day increment once they had been treated as permanent employees, and directed the authorities to calculate and release the resulting pension and retiral benefits within 30 days.
why_it_matters: Extends the 'notional increment' protection recognised in Mundinamani to employees who started out as daily wagers, confirming that an employee's origin as a daily-wage worker cannot be used retrospectively to strip away retirement-day benefits once permanency has been conferred.

case_name: Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. v. Nectar Life Care & Anr.
citation: Commercial IP Suit (L) No. 28038 of 2025
holding_summary: Sun Pharma sued Ahmedabad-based Nectar Life Care and its sister concern Kashmik Formulations, alleging that drug names including L-HISTACT-M, HISTACT, OMENEC and SNIZACT were deceptively similar to its registered marks HISTAC and OMESEC (both Class 5). Justice Madhav J. Jamdar recorded a consent settlement under which the defendants agreed to permanently stop manufacturing, selling or dealing in seven identified product names, withdraw Nectar's pending trademark application for SNIZACT within seven days, acknowledge Sun Pharma's rights in HISTAC and OMESEC without challenging their validity, destroy remaining stock bearing the impugned marks, and pay litigation costs.
why_it_matters: Illustrates that pharmaceutical trademark disputes over phonetically or visually similar drug names are frequently resolved through detailed consent terms rather than contested trials, letting originator companies secure binding commitments — including withdrawal of pending applications — without a final adjudication on infringement.

case_name: V-Guard Industries Limited v. Ashok Kumar Trading as R.K. Industries & Ors.
citation: CS(COMM) 1117/2026, Delhi High Court, order dated 13 October 2026
holding_summary: Justice Vikas Mahajan granted V-Guard Industries an ex parte interim injunction restraining R.K. Industries (traced only as 'Ashok Kumar' after the address on its packaging proved incomplete) and associated sellers from manufacturing or selling electrical wires in black-and-yellow packaging the Court found prima facie imitated V-Guard's own trade dress, used since 2017 and covered by trademark and copyright registrations; the restraint extends to any colourable imitation of that colour combination and binds the named sellers' distributors and dealers. The Court separately directed marketplaces IndiaMart and TradeIndia to take down the listed product pages within one week of being notified of the order, with compliance affidavits due two weeks after that.
why_it_matters: Another example of Delhi High Court extending an ex parte trade-dress injunction to the e-commerce marketplaces hosting the infringing listings, not just the seller, with a firm one-week takedown deadline — a template remedy for brand owners whose distinctive packaging is being copied through online marketplace listings.

case_name: ACC Limited v. ACC Steel
citation: Karnataka High Court, Division Bench, order dated 1 October 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices D.K. Singh and H. Shanthi Bhushan dismissed ACC Steel's appeal against a Bengaluru Rural commercial court decree (in a suit filed by ACC Limited, user of the 'ACC' mark for cement since 1938) restraining ACC Steel from using 'ACC' as a trademark or as part of its company/trade name on its steel products. The Court rejected ACC Steel's argument that the dispute should be confined to the different trademark classes the two companies' goods fall under, holding that 'ACC' is a well-known trademark whose protection is not limited by class. The commercial court's decree, left undisturbed, also directed ACC Steel to amend its trade name and deliver up infringing material for destruction, though it had declined to award the Rs. 10 lakh damages sought for want of material to quantify them.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a well-known trademark's protection is not confined to the trademark class in which it is registered — a defendant cannot escape infringement liability merely by pointing to a different class of goods, a recurring defence where an established brand's initials are reused on an unrelated product line.

case_name: Homebuyers v. Sai Enterprises & Super Construction
citation: MahaRERA, Pune (Adjudicating Officer R.K. Malabade), order reported 10 October 2026
court: Maharashtra Real Estate Regulatory Authority (MahaRERA), Pune
holding_summary: Homebuyers had booked a flat from Super Construction in 2010 and paid Rs. 17.49 lakh; after development rights passed to Sai Enterprises, the buyers were asked to accept a refund instead of a flat, which they refused, insisting on allotment. MahaRERA had already directed the developers (on or about 31 October 2025) to allot a flat and execute an Agreement for Sale, but by then all units in the project had been sold, leaving no flat available and no 'fit person' appointable under MahaRERA Circular No. 50. For non-compliance with that order, the Adjudicating Officer imposed a lump-sum penalty of Rs. 10 lakh on Sai Enterprises and Super Construction under Section 63 of RERA, with a recovery warrant under Section 40(1) to issue for the penalty, accrued interest on the amount paid, and Rs. 20,000 in costs if not deposited within two months.
why_it_matters: Shows that selling out a project does not let a developer (or a successor who takes over development rights) off the hook for an unmet MahaRERA allotment order — once compliance becomes impossible, MahaRERA will still impose the maximum Section 63 lump-sum penalty rather than simply treating a refund as adequate substitute performance.

case_name: Prem Highway Services v. Union of India & Ors.
citation: Civil Writ Jurisdiction Case No. 16335 of 2025, Patna High Court, order dated 12 August 2026
holding_summary: A petroleum dealer challenged a Rs. 1,25,71,936 GST liability raised under an assessment order dated 29 April 2024, arguing its sales of motor spirit and high-speed diesel were non-GST goods still taxable only under the State VAT regime, since no notification under Section 9(2) of the CGST Act has ever brought these items into GST. A Division Bench of Justices Anil Kumar Sinha and Vikash Kumar held that imposing GST on items outside the GST net goes to the root of the adjudicating authority's jurisdiction, quashed the assessment, and remanded the matter, directing the petitioner to appear with its reply and documents within 20 days and the authority to pass a fresh, reasoned order after a personal hearing within two months.
why_it_matters: A reusable jurisdictional challenge for petroleum dealers and allied businesses still facing GST demands on motor spirit, diesel or other non-GST petroleum products: the absence of any Section 9(2) notification bringing these goods into GST is, on this ruling, a threshold defect that can get an assessment quashed outright rather than merely reduced.

case_name: TGSPDCL & TGNPDCL v. Lanco Kondapalli Power Limited
citation: Telangana High Court, interim order dated 14 October 2026
holding_summary: Telangana's two distribution companies sought protection after Lanco Kondapalli Power Limited uploaded four invoices totalling Rs. 24,15,84,988 to the Centre's PRAAPTI late-payment portal, which the discoms said related to historical financing and procurement-cost claims rather than current power supply, and so fell outside the 2022 Late Payment Surcharge Rules' coercive-recovery mechanism. Justice E.V. Venugopal restrained any coercive action on the four disputed invoices, with the protection running until 28 October 2026, the date on which the discoms' own APTEL appeal against a June 2026 CERC order (which had ruled in Lanco's favour on the underlying financing/procurement-cost claims) was listed for hearing.
why_it_matters: Confirms that the PRAAPTI portal's automatic late-payment-surcharge and coercive-recovery machinery is not available for historical or disputed claims still pending challenge before APTEL or a regulator — a discom facing a PRAAPTI upload over a claim under appeal has a basis to seek interim High Court protection rather than paying first and litigating later.

case_name: Mausam Meena v. Flipkart Internet Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, South-II, Delhi, order dated 31 July 2026
court: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, South-II, Delhi
holding_summary: The complainant ordered a Realme Narzo 50A smartphone for Rs. 10,574 through Flipkart, sold by Luminary Lifestyle, but the sealed package delivered on 25 October 2021 was found on video to contain bars of Lifebuoy soap instead of the phone. Flipkart argued it was merely an intermediary marketplace and that liability lay with the seller, pointing also to the complainant's return history and an alleged failure to furnish ID and product images on request. The Commission rejected the intermediary defence, holding Flipkart liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, and directed a refund of Rs. 10,574 with 7% annual interest plus Rs. 5,000 for mental harassment and Rs. 5,000 in litigation costs, with 8% interest to apply from the date of the order if not paid within 60 days.
why_it_matters: Another in a consistent line of consumer-forum rulings holding e-commerce marketplaces directly liable for wrong-item deliveries despite an intermediary defence — platforms facilitating paid transactions and collecting commission cannot deflect liability onto the seller alone once a wrong, lower-value item is shown to have been delivered.

case_name: FSSAI recall directions against Nilgiri Oil & Allied Industries (Shalimar's Chef Coriander Powder) and Aquagri Processing Pvt. Ltd. (carrageenan)
citation: FSSAI regulatory recall order (not litigation)
holding_summary: FSSAI directed Nilgiri Oil & Allied Industries to recall its Shalimar's Chef brand coriander powder after a regulatory sample, and a retest sample taken on the company's appeal, both failed for pesticide residues above permissible limits. In a parallel action, FSSAI directed Aquagri Processing Pvt. Ltd. to withdraw its carrageenan from the market after a sample was found to contain cadmium above the permissible standard, a finding the Referral Food Laboratory upheld on the company's appeal.
why_it_matters: A reminder that FSSAI's unsafe-classification findings are now being confirmed on referral/appeal testing in both cases before the recall is enforced, so a food business cannot treat an adverse sample result as open to informal dispute — it must engage the statutory retest and appeal process promptly or face a market withdrawal.

case_name: Dickey Special Situation Investment Trust-DSSF Series 2 & Prudent ARC Ltd. v. Manish Agarwal (Liquidator, Worlds Window Exim Pvt. Ltd.) & Ors.
citation: NCLAT, order on or about 12 October 2026, affirming NCLT (New Delhi) order dated 14 August 2026 rejecting the resolution plan; exact Company Appeal number not independently confirmed from available secondary sources
holding_summary: The NCLAT dismissed appeals by the successful resolution applicant and by a financial creditor holding about 94.86% of CoC voting shares, upholding the NCLT's rejection of a Rs. 7 crore resolution plan for Worlds Window Exim Pvt. Ltd. The tribunal held that a plan offering less than liquidation value is not illegal in itself, but this plan failed to satisfy the mandatory requirements of Section 30(2) of the IBC read with Regulation 39(3)(a) of the CIRP Regulations because it did not show how it addressed the corporate debtor's cause of default. The NCLT's direction for liquidation and an investigation into the company's affairs, including avoidance applications, was left undisturbed.
why_it_matters: CoC approval and a high voting share cannot cure a resolution plan that omits a reasoned explanation of the corporate debtor's cause of default — resolution applicants and committees must build this into the plan itself, not treat it as a formality, or risk the plan being rejected even after CoC approval.
